summary: Defines a set of structured header fields that mailing list software can add to messages, using URLs to describe list commands such as subscribe and unsubscribe. This lets mail clients offer automated tools for list functions.

plainLanguage.summary: Mailing lists each have their own way of being joined, left and asked for help, and a user has to learn those rules one list at a time. This RFC fixes a small set of email header fields, all named List-something, that a list fills in with addresses. A mail client reads them and can then offer a Subscribe or Unsubscribe button that works whatever the list runs.

questions: how do email clients unsubscribe from lists
what are the list-id style mailing list headers
subtitle: Standard List-* header fields that let mail programs show Subscribe, Unsubscribe and Help buttons for any mailing list.

tldr.problem: Every mailing list manager has its own syntax for subscribing, unsubscribing and asking for help, so a mail client cannot show the user the right command, and the user has to learn each list's rules by hand.
tldr.mechanism: A mailing list adds a set of List- header fields to each message it sends, and each field holds one or more URLs, usually mailto URLs, that describe or perform the command. The client picks the leftmost URL it supports.
tldr.outcome: The three core fields, List-Help, List-Subscribe and List-Unsubscribe, give every list the same way of advertising its commands, and the three secondary fields, List-Post, List-Owner and List-Archive, cover the rest.

facts.label: URLs per field
facts.value: One or more, in order of preference

facts.label: Occurrences per message
facts.value: At most one of each field

today:
RFC 2369 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, so it remains the document that defines the List- header fields for mailing list commands.

The memo itself describes its own reach: it is a set of optional header fields that a list may include, and the List-Help field is the one a list manager can include on its own. It also records that the use of these fields does not remove the requirement to support the -Request command address for mailing lists.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This is a proposal for additional header fields to be added to email messages sent by email distribution lists. The content of each new field is typically a URL, usually a mailto URL, which locates the relevant information or performs the command directly. Mail transfer agents generating the header fields should usually include a mailto based command, in addition to any other protocols used, so that users without access to non-mail based protocols are still served.

Implementing these fields is optional, though significant functionality and convenience can be gained by including them. Many list managers, especially as the proposal first gains acceptance, may choose to implement only one or two of the fields. The List-Help field is the most useful individual field, because it provides an access point to detailed user support information and accommodates almost all existing list manager command sets. The List-Subscribe and List-Unsubscribe fields are also very useful, but cannot describe some list manager syntaxes, namely those that require variable substitution.

The description of command syntax that the fields provide can be used by mail client applications to give users simplified and consistent access to email distribution list functions, in the form of menu items, push buttons or other user interface elements. The intent is to simplify the user experience by providing a common interface to the often cryptic and varied mailing list manager commands. The use of these fields does not remove the requirement to support the -Request command address for mailing lists.
sections.plainLanguage: Each list server has its own commands, and they are not alike. This RFC gives lists a common way of advertising those commands in the message itself, so that a mail program can offer the same button for every list. Using URLs rather than a new command language means the client can reuse the URL handling it already has.

sections.title: The Command Syntax
sections.content:
The list header fields are subject to the encoding and character restrictions for mail headers described in RFC 822, and the URL content is further restricted to the set of URL safe characters.

The contents of the list header fields mostly consist of angle-bracket enclosed URLs, with internal whitespace being ignored. Mail transfer agents must not insert whitespace within the brackets, but client applications should treat any whitespace that a poorly behaved mail transfer agent has inserted as characters to ignore.

A list of multiple, alternate URLs may be given as a comma-separated list of angle-bracket enclosed URLs, in order of preference from left to right. The client application should use the leftmost protocol it supports, or knows how to reach by a separate application, so that a protocol such as http can be given while mailto support is still provided for clients without access to non-mail protocols. The client should use only one of the available URLs for a command, falling back to another only if the first one used failed.

Using URLs means the fields work with applications that already support URLs, and they gain whatever the URL standard gains. It also gives access to several transport protocols, although mailto is expected to be the focus of most use of the list header fields; non-mailto protocols should be considered in light of users who have email only and no web access.

Command syntaxes that require the client to fill in variable fields, such as including the user's own email address inside a command, are not supported. Systems using such syntaxes should still take advantage of the List-Help field, either to give the user detailed instructions or to provide access to some form of structured command interface such as an HTML based form. The document records that supporting variables was judged too difficult and would compromise the likelihood of implementation.

To allow for future extension, client applications must follow three rules when handling the contents of these fields. If the content of the field, after any leading whitespace and comments, begins with any character other than the opening angle bracket, the field should be ignored. Any characters following an angle-bracket enclosed URL should be ignored, unless a comma is the first non-whitespace, non-comment character after the closing angle bracket. And if a comma-separated sub-item within the field is not an angle-bracket enclosed URL, the remainder of the field, that sub-item and all later ones, should be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: A field holds URLs in angle brackets, and a list of them separated by commas means alternatives, best first. The client tries the first one it understands. Because the rules for parsing are fixed, a field that arrives in an unexpected shape is ignored rather than guessed at, so a future extension cannot break today's clients.

sections.title: The List Header Fields
sections.content:
The document presents header fields that give the command syntax for the core and key secondary functions of most email distribution lists. The fields implemented on a given list should be included on all messages distributed by the list, including command responses to individual users, and on other messages where the message clearly applies to one distinct list. There must be no more than one of each field present in any given message, and these fields must only be generated by mailing lists, not by end users.

List-Help is the most important of the header fields, and a list manager could include only this one, because by definition it should direct the user to complete instructions for all other commands. The URL would typically request the help file for the list, perhaps with an HTML form for list commands, or point at an instructive website.

List-Unsubscribe describes the command, preferably using mail, that directly unsubscribes the user by removing them from the list. List-Subscribe describes the command that requests addition to the list.

List-Post describes the method for posting to the list. This is typically the address of the list, but may be a moderator or some other form of submission. For the special case of a list that does not allow posting, such as an announcements list, the field may contain the special value NO. List-Owner identifies the path to contact a human administrator for the list, which may be an administrator for the list, the mail system administrator, or anyone else who can handle user contact. There is no need to specify List-Owner if it is the same person as the postmaster. List-Archive describes how to access the archives for the list.
sections.plainLanguage: Six fields are defined. Three are the core ones: where to find help, how to join, and how to leave. The other three say where to post, who runs the list, and where the archive is. A list may include only some of them, but it must never include the same field twice in one message, and only a list may set them.

sections.title: Supporting Nested Lists
sections.content:
A list that is a sublist for another list in a nested mailing list hierarchy has to modify some of the List- header fields while leaving others as the parent list set them.

Sublists should remove the parent's List-Help, List-Subscribe, List-Unsubscribe and List-Owner fields and insert their own versions of those fields. If the sublist provides its own archive, it should replace the List-Archive with its own; otherwise it must leave the List-Archive field untouched. Depending on how postings to the list are handled, the sublist may replace the List-Post field, and whether it should is left to the individual list managers. If the intention is that postings should be distributed to all members of the primary list, List-Post should not be changed by a sublist in a way that makes postings reach only the members of the sublist.
sections.plainLanguage: When one list sits inside another, the inner list takes over the help, join, leave and owner fields and keeps its own, because those commands belong to the inner list. The archive field is only replaced if the inner list has an archive of its own, and the posting field is a decision for the list managers.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document says there are very few new security concerns generated by the proposal. Message headers are an existing standard designed to accommodate new types easily. There may be concern about multiple fields being inserted or headers being forged, but those are problems inherent in Internet email, not specific to this protocol, and the implications are relatively harmless.

Mail list processors should not allow any user-originated list header fields to pass through to their lists, lest they confuse the user and create security problems. On the client side there may be some concern about posts or commands being sent in error, so the user must have a chance to confirm any action before it is executed. In the case of mailto, it may be appropriate to create the correctly formatted message without sending it, so the user can see exactly what is happening and approve or discard it.

All the security considerations for the use of URLs apply equally here. Mail client applications should not support list header field URLs that could compromise the security of the user's system, which includes the file URL type, since it could potentially be used to trigger the execution of a local application on some user systems.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things need care. A list must not pass on header fields that a user put in the message, because a user could fake a Subscribe button. And the client must show the user the command it is about to send, so a mistake can be spotted before it goes out.

sections.title: Why the Design Is the Way It Is
sections.content:
Appendix A of the document records the alternatives that were considered and the reasons for the choices made. A single header field carrying all the command syntax was rejected: it would have required a new meta-syntax rather than the widely deployed URL syntax, every extra layer of complexity reduces the chance of implementation, and describing many commands in one field risks the field being modified by a server on route. Multiple fields are also easier for the client, since each command can be implemented independently and a list manager or client can implement a subset of the fields.

URLs were chosen over parameter lists because URLs are an established, flexible and widely used syntax that handles mailto, http and ftp, and because many clients already have functionality for recognising, parsing and evaluating URLs, either internally or by handing the request to a helper application. The document notes that this existing support let the authors add prototype list header functionality to existing mail clients without modifying their source code.

A standard command language supported by all list services would have cut the amount users had to learn, but such standardisation poses problems with multi-lingual support and the custom needs of individual lists, and was expected to be adopted slowly. Restricting the proposal to the core functions keeps the client implementation simple, which raises the chance of it being implemented.

Variable substitution was not supported. Variables would let the fields cover nearly every existing list manager, but they would measurably increase the complexity of the whole proposal and might force a redesign of the URL standard, and the use of variables in list service command syntaxes appears to be lessening and does not apply to all commands.

A specialised MIME part was considered and rejected, because most mail clients either do not support MIME or are not equipped to handle such parts, and it is not as easy for list servers to implement MIME as it is to implement new header fields. The authors were still looking for a way to describe list command syntax more fully in a MIME part. Subscribe and Unsubscribe were included because they are the key commands almost every list needs, while other commands such as digest mode are not as widely supported, and because users who have unsubscribed, changed address, or received a forwarded message may want to subscribe later.
sections.plainLanguage: The document explains its choices at length. The short version: one field per command, URLs instead of a new language, and only the handful of commands that every list has. Everything else was judged too complicated to implement, and something only a few list servers need was left out on purpose.

cells: Where to find instructions for all the other commands
The command that requests addition to the list
The command that removes the user from the list
How to post to the list, or the value NO when posting is not allowed
The path to contact a human administrator for the list
How to access the archives for the list

data.title: List-Unsubscribe and List-Subscribe examples
data.code:
List-Unsubscribe: <http://www.host.com/list.cgi?cmd=unsub&lst=list>,
    <mailto:list-request@host.com?subject=unsubscribe>

List-Subscribe: <mailto:list@host.com?subject=subscribe>
List-Subscribe: (Use this command to join the list)
    <mailto:list-manager@host.com?body=subscribe%20list>

List-Post: <mailto:moderator@host.com> (Postings are Moderated)
List-Post: NO (posting not allowed on this list)
